newsitem.title: USA: Death penalty no deterrent to violence - U.S. study.
newsitem.headline: Death penalty no deterrent to violence - U.S. study.

text.p: Twenty years after the U.S. Supreme Court reinstated the death penalty, almost all experts believe there is no evidence capital punishment deters violent crime, according to research released on Wednesday.

Researchers at the University of Florida surveyed 67 current and former presidents of the top three criminology professional organisations -- the American Society of Criminology, the Academy of Criminal Justice Sciences and the Law and Society Association -- and found that 90 percent felt that executing people to deter violent crime was a waste of both time and money.

"Among the experts there is overwhelming consensus that the death penalty never has been, is not and never could be a deterrent to homicide over and above long imprisonment," said Michael Radelet, chairman of the university's sociology department and an expert on death penalty issues.
"The rates of consensus were much higher on this question than I ever thought possible. We never see 90 percent of criminologists agree on anything," he said.
"The death penalty has nothing to do with crime rates. If politicians are serious about reducing high rates of criminal violence, they're barking up the wrong tree," Radelet said.

Gary Gilmore faced a Utah firing squad on Jan. 17, 1977, becoming the first person executed in the United States since the Supreme Court again legalised the death penalty in 1972. By Dec. 31, 1996, 357 other prisoners had been executed.

Radelet said that in assessing capital punishment, the public should keep in mind the difference between an effective deterrent -- which persuades someone not to commit a violent criminal act -- and an act of retribution, which is punishment for a criminal.

"Politicians who say we need the death penalty to cut the crime rate or arguments of that sort are simply wrong," Radelet said. Violent crime rates have risen and fallen regardless of how many people were sentenced to death.
He said people supported the death penalty fervently out of a desire for retribution and because they feared offenders would be released from prison after a short sentence if not put to death.

Radelet also said the death penalty was expensive, noting that the cost of an execution in Florida averaged about $3.2 million, mostly in trial costs, versus only about $600,000 to keep the prisoner locked up for life.
